response.evidence: There are about 33 Black or African American female applicants in the data. About 6 were denied (~18%), which is higher than the overall denial rate of roughly 10%. However, most of these denials line up with recorded risk factors. Four of the six had debt-to-income (DTI) ratios of 50-60%, a range where applicants of all races are denied about half the time. One had a loan-to-value (LTV) ratio above 100% with low income. Only one denial (DTI 41, income 158, LTV 90) has no obvious risk explanation. Black females with moderate DTI were mostly approved, including ones with high LTV (95-102%) and very low incomes. The data does show a higher raw denial rate for this group. But the sample is small, credit scores and other key underwriting factors are missing, and DTI largely explains the gap, so the data does not provide clear evidence of discrimination. It also cannot rule it out. This is observational data and cannot prove or disprove discrimination.

The dataset does not show statistically meaningful evidence of discrimination against Black or African American female applicants. My manual count found about 34 such applicants: 29 were originated and 5 were denied, a denial rate of roughly 15%. The overall denial rate across the dataset is approximately 9-10%, also counted manually. That gap is modest, and with only about 34 applicants a difference of 1-2 denials changes the rate by 3-6 points, so it is not statistically reliable. Some denials have plausible financial explanations, such as one applicant reporting $0 income. Others (e.g., $335K loan, DTI 40, LTV 70) look similar to approved files, but comparable White female applicants were also denied (e.g., DTI 44, LTV 70; DTI 48, LTV 70). Black or African American female applicants were approved even at high DTI (49%, >60%) and LTV up to 100-101.75%. The data lacks key underwriting variables such as credit score and employment history, so disparities cannot be attributed to race or sex. The data neither proves nor rules out discrimination; it only shows no clear disparate pattern.

Two of the four denials have clear risk factors: one had a 50-60% debt-to-income ratio with income of 65, and another had income of 46 on a 145000 loan. The fourth denial (income 372, debt-to-income 20-30%, loan-to-value 60) is not explained by the variables shown, but other groups also have similar unexplained denials. Black or African American women with high debt-to-income (up to 49%, and one at 50-60%) and loan-to-value of 97-102% were approved. The data lacks credit scores and other underwriting factors, so discrimination cannot be confirmed or ruled out, but this dataset shows no clear pattern of it.

My count from the rows: there are about 33 Black or African American female applicants, and 7 were denied (about 21%). That is higher than the dataset-wide denial rate, which I estimate at roughly 8-10% without a full tally. However, 6 of the 7 denials had debt-to-income ratios of 50% or higher ('50%-60%' or '>60%'). Applicants of every race and sex in those DTI ranges are denied at high rates, and those with '>60%' DTI are denied in nearly every case. Among Black female applicants with DTI below 50%, only 1 of about 27 was denied (about 4%), which is comparable to or lower than other groups with similar DTI. Approved Black female applicants include high-loan, high-LTV cases with DTI in the 45-49 range, similar to approved applicants of other groups. So the raw gap appears explained by debt-to-income ratio, not race or sex. Confidence is moderate because the subgroup is small, the counts were made by hand, and the data lacks variables such as credit score and denial reasons.

The disparity is worth investigating with a larger sample and full underwriting data, but it is not clear evidence of discrimination on its own.

Both denials had loan-to-value ratios above 100% (300% and 102%), a common underwriting risk factor. Black female applicants with higher-risk profiles were still approved, including DTI of 50%-60% (2 cases) and LTV of 97%-100% (several cases). So the data shows no disparity in outcomes. Confidence is moderate because the sample is small, key underwriting variables such as credit score are missing, and outcome data alone cannot prove or rule out discrimination.
